To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the fluorescence yield of nitrogen in air is a function of wavelength, pressure, temperature, and the water vapor content of air.

(i) the nitrogen emission is proportional to the pressure, (ii) the nitrogen emission depends linearly on the temperature, and (iii) the nitrogen emission decreases with increasing water vapor pressure.

the nitrogen fluorescence emission at 300 nm is proportional to the atmospheric pressure at the altitude of the emission, that it is proportional to the nitrogen density in air, that it is independent of the temperature, that it depends on the wavelength, that the collisional de- excitation of the nitrogen molecules by oxygen is negligible, that the collision de-excitation by hydrogen is important, and that the collision de- excitation by water vapor is important.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the description of the nitrogen fluorescence in air for air shower observations in the atmosphere.
the description of the nitrogen fluorescence in air for the purpose of a common treatment in air shower reconstruction.
the development of a common description of nitrogen fluorescence in air for application to cosmic ray air shower analyses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the emission process is well-understood, but the experimental uncertainties of some parameters are still rather large.
a description of fluorescence emission is possible with a sufficient accuracy for most applications.
the fluorescence emission of nitrogen in air is well-understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the emission procedure is not well understood yet, in particular the role of water vapor in the collisional deexcitation of the excited nitrogen molecules.

the fluorescence yields are well known and can be described in a common way for the wavelength region between 280 and 450 nm, which is the region used for fluorescence observations in the air showers.
a common description of the nitrogen fluorescence for air shower observations is feasible, and that the fluorescence emission is well understood for the most important atmospheric conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we are able to provide a description of the fluorescence yield which is valid for a wide range of atmospheric conditions.
a common treatment of nitrogen fluorescence emission in the atmosphere is indeed possible, and that the resulting fluorescence yields agree within the uncertainties.
the fluorescence yield is not constant, but depends on the atmospheric conditions.
